headline: The database is not under load: the app statements that cost production the most add up to about 39 minutes of database time in 78 days, and the slowest averages 145 ms. The bloat is in how often data is asked for and how much comes back: most of the work is done for nobody. 63% of the listed database time is the scheduler calling routes that find nothing to do, 75% of all transactions are two idle polls, the most expensive app query reads every published page whole to find one page or a few titles, and reads marked "use cache" for hours still ran 500 to 1,000 times a day each because that cache lives in one function instance and every deploy empties it. None of this hurts at 60 stores, but several shapes grow with stores times ticks, and most are a day or a few days to fix.

clean: src/db/client.ts: one pool per instance (max 5, idle 5 s) attached to Vercel's lifecycle, node-postgres chosen for the transaction pooler with the reason written down (D37), no named prepared statements anywhere (0 hits for .prepare( on the database).
Statement and lock limits are the role's (15 s, 5 s) and a longer one is taken with set local inside a transaction (longerTimeout, client.ts:89-92), never a plain set through the pooler.
Transactions around single reads are rare: 12 of 391 by their text, each with a reason (a timeout raised for one report, an advisory lock held for a run).
Counting by loading rows is rare: 6 heuristic hits in 1,648 selects; counts are done with count(*) in SQL.
The read replica (replicaDb, client.ts:105-110) is built but off, used by one module (analytics-totals.ts) and costs nothing while READ_DATABASE_URL is unset. With 102 orders it is not needed.
publishedPageNames (pages.ts:713-735) pulls titles out of the JSON in SQL instead of fetching documents: the right shape, and the model for DQ-2.
Queues are claimed with for update skip locked (integrations.ts:1033-1039, cookie-scans.ts:78-83), so overlapping runs do not double-send.
Several dispatcher jobs already ask only for stores where the feature is set up before doing anything (staff-alerts.ts:1020-1023 and 1122-1127).

The admin's session, account and membership reads are wrapped in React cache() (auth.ts:121, 215, 354, 407), and cart, checkout and order share one read per request through perRequest() (request-memo.ts).

status_checks is pruned at 91 days (status.ts:265, STATUS_DAYS = 90 in src/lib/status.ts:17); the statistics show 0 deletes only because no row is that old yet (20,547 rows is about 12 days of 6 checks every 5 minutes). It will level off near 157,000 rows.
The proxy's two store reads are kept 10 s per instance (redirect-resolve.ts:203-232, house-switch.ts:31-43) and neither appears among production's most-called statements.

findings.title: Nine routes are called every minute to ask the database whether there is work, and there almost never is
findings.evidence: pg_cron schedules nine jobs with '* * * * *', each a net.http_post that also reads the cron secret from Vault. Production: 352,514 calls, 3,974 s, the single largest item (63% of listed time). cron_jobs says the routes last took 0 to 72 ms: nothing to do. What an idle minute still runs, read from the code: theme-shots reads every published theme with its whole snapshot (35,101 calls, 101 s, 348,763 rows), the theme contents (store-starters.ts:337), the showcase stores and the stored queue, then opens a transaction with an advisory lock to claim (71,422 lock calls, a third of all production transactions), then prunes; this although publishing a theme already queues its shots (theme-shots.ts:421). cookie-scan runs two updates (65,200 calls each) and a CTE over every open store (49,338 calls, 192 s) that causes 1.1 M sequential scans of cookie_scans (962 M rows read), for about 9 scans a day (60 sites, one a week, SCAN_EVERY at cookie-scans.ts:33). integrations runs seven sub-jobs, among them a claim and a prune delete on integration_deliveries (66,533 calls each) which has never held a row. autopilot reads the pause switch three times a minute (69,075 calls). Each route also writes one ledger upsert a minute.
findings.cost: 12,960 function invocations a day; about 94% of 3,974 s of database time so far; 71,422 lock transactions; 1.1 M sequential scans; roughly 60,000 statements a day that return nothing (estimate from 3 to 9 statements per route per minute).
findings.who_pays: The database and the server (function invocations); nobody benefits.
findings.fix: Put the test in the scheduler's own SQL so no HTTP call is made when idle: select net.http_post(...) where exists (select 1 from commerce.theme_shots where status in ('waiting','running')), and the same with one exists per route (queued cookie scans, pending deliveries or workflow runs or inbound emails, packs wanted, page jobs, looks, Dream Factory runs, broadcasts due, autopilot plans due). Start the weekly cookie scans from a separate hourly job. Stop re-deriving the wanted theme shots each minute: keep the call at theme-shots.ts:421 and a daily sweep. Move the two prune deletes (integrations.ts:1062, platform-integrations.ts) to the daily job. Keep the lateness check of REL-06 with a heartbeat written by the scheduler's SQL itself (an upsert into commerce.cron_jobs), so a route that is not called does not read as late.
findings.saving: Estimate: about 97% of scheduler calls (12,900 of 13,248 a day), most of 3,974 s per 78 days, about a third of all transactions, and the 1.1 M sequential scans of cookie_scans. Reaction time stays one minute.
findings.risk: A wrong "due" test leaves work waiting. Keep one unconditional run every 15 minutes per route for the first weeks, and compare.
findings.already_tracked: no (docs/capacity.md:201-202 only says heavy work gets a route of its own; psi-followups REL-06, done, is the ledger this must keep)

findings.title: Every published page is read whole to find one page or a few titles
findings.evidence: listPublishedPages() selects id, slug, published (the whole document), published_at, first_published_at for every published page of an owner, parses each with zod, then looks up library alt texts for every picture on every page (withPageAlts, with the URL list sent twice as separate parameters). It has 37 call sites (rg). Most then do .find() for one id (front page, products page, role page, legal pages, checkout terms) or read only titles: the platform's header and footer menus load every page and every article whole to build a map of id, slug and title (platform-navigation.ts:138-146); a store's footer loads them all to print up to five legal titles (legal-links.ts:24-29). Production: 79,778 calls, 781 s, 2,334,038 rows, 29 rows a call. It is the most expensive app statement, 33% of the listed app time. publishedPageNames (pages.ts:713) already shows the slim shape.
findings.cost: 781 s in 78 days, 9.8 ms a call. Estimate: about 90 KB a call (29 rows at about 3 KB, from pages being 9.1 MB for 1,389 rows with draft and published), parsed each time; the same list is held once per cache entry. Part of the 43,240 sequential scans of media follows from the alt lookup.
findings.who_pays: The server on every cold render of a page's frame; the database; a visitor waits for it on a first view after a deploy.
findings.fix: Split it in two cached reads under the same tag. (1) publishedPageIndex(owner, type): id, slug, title and translated titles, markets, the search and AI flags, the two dates, all taken with JSON operators in SQL, no document. (2) publishedPageById(owner, id): one document with its alt texts. Move the callers that find one id to (2) and the menus, legal links, sitemap and robots to (1). Keep the full list only for generateStaticParams, which needs slugs alone, so it also moves to (1).
findings.saving: Estimate: most of 781 s (rows shrink from whole documents to a few short columns, or to one row), the parse of 29 documents per call, and the alt lookup for pages not being drawn.
findings.risk: A caller that silently needed another field of the content. The types will show it: PublishedPage.content disappears from the index type.
findings.already_tracked: no (code review step 3.9, Open, is the same idea for products: "Stop reading the whole catalogue for one page")

findings.title: "Where is this picture used" scans every page's text for each picture, and the job re-checks every picture daily
findings.evidence: mediaUses() joins each picture to every page of the site and tests position(m.url in pg.draft::text) and the same on published, so both documents of every page are cast to text per picture; it does the same over entries, menus, saved parts, theme looks and settings in 12 union branches. Production: 1,831 calls at 145 ms, and other shapes 43 at 925 ms, 198 at 133 ms, 205 at 66 ms, 776 at 47 ms: about 382 s in all, the second most expensive app statement. The five-minute media job calls it for every picture whose vector is older than a day, "so what uses an item is kept current" (media-library.ts:810, 815), then only moves the date on unchanged ones (827-831): media_embeddings shows 13,414 updates on 468 rows. The stale check itself ran 49,842 times.
findings.cost: About 382 s in 78 days; up to 925 ms a call, which nears the size where an owner's media library page feels slow. It grows with pictures times pages times page size.
findings.who_pays: The database every five minutes for every site with media; an owner opening the media library.
findings.fix: Step 1 (S): in embedMedia drop the daily re-check unless something that can hold a picture changed since the vector's date (one max(updated_at) over the site's pages, products, menus and entries). Step 2 (M): keep uses in a table media_uses(media_id, source, ref_id) written when a page, product, menu, entry or theme is saved (pageImageUrls() already lists a page's pictures) and read it in the library, the embeddings and the alt-text job; run today's query once a night to reconcile.
findings.saving: Estimate: at least 80% of the 382 s and nearly all 13,414 re-stamps after step 1; the library's read becomes an index lookup after step 2.
findings.risk: A writer that forgets to record a use leaves "Used in" stale until the nightly reconcile. The list of places is already written in one comment (media-compress.ts:205-206).

findings.title: Each request for an AI connection sums the store's whole month of AI usage
findings.evidence: aiFor() has 92 call sites. For a store on the platform's key whose plan has a limit it calls aiRoomLeft(), which sums every ai_usage row of the month with a lateral price lookup per row. The one-minute memo (limits.ts:122, 136-139) lives in one function instance, so it rarely helps. ai_usage has no cost column. Production: 6,782 calls at 37 ms and 1,732 at 57 ms, about 352 s, the third most expensive app statement, for a table of 19,104 rows. The cost per call grows with the month's usage.
findings.cost: About 352 s in 78 days; 37 to 57 ms added in front of AI features and of jobs that loop over stores.
findings.who_pays: The database; a shopper or owner waiting for an AI answer; each five-minute job that asks per store.
findings.fix: Do what storage_bytes already does at limits.ts:142-150: month to date = the daily totals already measured in store_usage_daily plus today's rows only. Re-measure the month when a model's price is added for past dates.
findings.saving: Estimate: about 90% of the 352 s (one day's rows instead of a month's), and the cost stops growing through the month.
findings.risk: Past days are as good as the nightly measure. A price added later for an unpriced model must trigger a re-measure, or the limit reads low.

findings.title: The five-minute dispatcher runs 84 jobs at once on 5 connections, and several redo real work every tick
findings.evidence: runJobs() starts every job with Promise.all (cron-runs.ts:117) while the pool holds 5 connections with a 5 s connect timeout (client.ts:68, 70). Each job writes its own ledger upsert: 457,349 + 107,700 calls, 84 s. Jobs that do real work on every tick whatever changed: embeddings recomputes an md5 over title, terms and description of every active product translation of every store (10,201 calls, 148 s) and calls commerce.store_is_active() per row, a SQL function with a SET clause, which Postgres does not inline (this fits the 12 M index scans on the 60-row stores table; the function is used in 67 places in 43 files). invoices calls two issuing functions for the same stuck store on every tick for up to 120 days (9,909 calls each, 167 s, for 102 orders in all). bonus_expire_due ran 11,790 times at 2.1 ms on tables that never held a row. vat-labels asks the database 4,035 times at 7.3 ms whether it is within 10 minutes of a country's midnight.
findings.cost: At least 168 statements every five minutes when idle (84 jobs and 84 ledger writes); about 400 s of listed database time; the jobs' own times sum to about 12.5 s a tick because they queue for 5 connections.
findings.who_pays: The database and one function every five minutes. The risk is paid later: when the queue for a connection passes 5 s, jobs fail with a connect timeout.
findings.fix: (a) Write the ledger once after the jobs finish, as one multi-row upsert. (b) Give each job a cadence (prunes daily, trials hourly) and a cheap "due" test; evaluate all tests in one statement and run only the due jobs, at most 5 at a time. (c) Embeddings: mark a product dirty on save (the save already calls refreshStoreEmbeddings, embeddings.ts:126-130) and run the full hash check nightly; join stores instead of calling store_is_active() per row. (d) Invoices: a next-try time with backoff, and a try at once when the seller's details are saved. (e) VAT labels: decide the midnight window in code from the 28 countries' time zones.
findings.saving: Estimate: idle statements per tick from 168 or more to under 20; 24,192 ledger writes a day to 288; most of 148 s (embeddings) and 167 s (invoices).
findings.risk: A job with too long a cadence or a wrong due test runs late. cron_jobs already records every run, so lateness shows on the platform home.
findings.already_tracked: no (psi-followups REL-06, done, built the ledger and runJobs; it set no cadence or budget)

findings.title: The knowledge job reads every page whole every five minutes and re-cuts pages that have no text, forever
findings.evidence: For every site with its chat agent on, syncPageKnowledge() selects every published page and article with its whole published document (three statement shapes in production: 2,571 + 17,955 + 3,608 calls; the first returns 40 rows a call at 16 ms). It compares versions in code. A page whose text cuts to no passages (cutPassages returns [] at lib/knowledge.ts:65) has no chunk, so its stored version is null, never matches, and replacePassages() opens a transaction, deletes nothing and inserts nothing, on every tick. Production: 91,200 calls of delete from knowledge_chunks where page_id = $1 deleted 782 rows in all. That is about 4 such pages per tick (91,200 over 22,464 ticks) and 42% of all 216,877 transactions.
findings.cost: 91,200 empty transactions (273,600 round trips: begin, delete, commit); about 200 KB of page documents sent to the function each tick for the platform's site alone (estimate: 40 rows at about 5 KB); 542 ms of the dispatcher's run.
findings.who_pays: The database and the dispatcher function, every five minutes.
findings.fix: Keep what was cut in a small table knowledge_sources(page_id or entry_id, version, path), written also when there are no passages. Choose the pages to cut in SQL (published_at newer than the kept version, or the path changed) and fetch the document only for those. Call it from publishing a page and keep the job as an hourly net.
findings.saving: Measured count: 91,200 transactions and their round trips go to zero. Estimate: the whole-document read happens only when something was published.
findings.risk: Low. A missed publish is caught by the hourly run.
findings.already_tracked: no (docs/rules/storefront.md:408-411 states that the five-minute cron does this; the fix keeps it as the net)

findings.title: A page's frame asks about 20 questions each time its cache is cold, and the cache is cold far more often than the code assumes
findings.evidence: Next's own guide: with the default handler, on serverless "cache entries typically don't persist across requests", and no entry carries over a deploy because the key includes the build id. The repo has 85 "use cache" directives, no "use cache: remote" and no cacheHandlers. The last two days show 27 and 74 commits to main (git log), each a deploy. Production agrees: statements issued only from functions cached for hours ran 540 to 1,020 times a day each, for example the cookie scan result (70,257), cookie notes on an empty table (70,278), the modal check (68,878, 121 s), platform settings (53,887), the platform's menus (69,938). Reading PlatformRoot and what it calls gives about 21 statements for the frame alone: 8 for menus and names, 4 for header and footer, 5 for the consent banner, and settings, search texts, text styles and the site store. siteCookies() awaits its 7 or 8 reads one after another (site-cookies.ts:89-121). usesRememberedModals() runs jsonb_path_exists over every published page of the site to produce one boolean.
findings.cost: About 20 round trips before a page's own content on each cold render (estimate: 20 to 60 ms in the same region, not measured); 121 s of database time for the modal check alone.
findings.who_pays: The first visitor of a page after each deploy or cache expiry; the database.
findings.fix: Budget every cached read as if it were uncached. (1) Run siteCookies' independent reads with one Promise.all. (2) Keep the modal answer where pages are published: a stored generated column on pages (jsonb_path_exists is immutable) with a partial index, or a flag written by savePage. (3) Read a site's frame in one statement (settings, menus, page index from DQ-2, term names, header and footer, cookie facts). Do not add a remote cache for these: Next's guide says it gains little for operations under 50 ms, and it empties on each deploy too.
findings.saving: Estimate: a cold frame goes from about 20 statements to 3 or 4; 121 s of jsonb scans become an index lookup.
findings.risk: One larger read is refreshed by more tags. Keep the same tags on it, so nothing shows stale.
findings.already_tracked: partly: code review step 3.8 (Open) cuts round trips for cart and checkout only

findings.title: "is not distinct from" on store_id keeps the index from serving the hottest reads
findings.evidence: 145 uses in 52 files, 122 on store_id in 40 files. The ten that run most: pages.ts:71 (ownedBy, behind 79,778 calls), pages.ts:695 and 697 (67,601), pages.ts:728 and 733 (57,930), taxonomy.ts:60 (130,816), cookie-scans.ts:96 and 98 (49,338; 1.1 M sequential scans), site-cookies.ts:46 (70,257) and :55 (70,278), page-modals.ts:23 (68,878), content-grid.ts:266, support-email.ts:267 (a join, 40,141), then menus.ts, forms.ts, content-types.ts, saved-parts.ts and site-tools.ts with 5 to 10 each. EXPLAIN on the local scratch database (PostgreSQL 16.15, sequential scans off): with is not distinct from, store_id is only a Filter; with store_id = $1 or store_id is null it is an Index Cond on pages_store_slug_key. Production: pages 199,789 sequential scans reading 203 M rows, cookie_scans 1.1 M reading 962 M, terms 183,724 reading 11 M. Four files already branch correctly (chat-agent.ts:71, media-library.ts:77, knowledge.ts:29, google-reviews.ts:38).
findings.cost: Cheap per call today (1,389 pages), but every such read is a scan of the whole table: about 1.2 billion rows read by sequential scan on these three tables in 78 days. It grows with all stores' rows, not the one store's.
findings.who_pays: The database, on every page render and every cron minute.
findings.fix: One shared helper, owned(storeId, column), that writes column = $1 for a store and column is null for the platform, as those four files do. Move the hot ten first. For the two joins of column to column (cookie-scans.ts:96-98, support-email.ts:267) write the store branch and the platform branch as a union. Add a scan test that fails for a new is not distinct from on store_id. This keeps the rule in docs/rules/storefront.md:179 (one query serves a store and the platform's null) and changes only how it is written.
findings.saving: Estimate: the sequential scans of pages, terms and cookie_scans become index scans of one store's rows; little time saved at today's size, and the cost stops growing with other stores' data.
findings.risk: Low. Passing null into the = branch would return nothing, which is why the helper branches in code. Each move is covered by the existing tests of that read.
findings.already_tracked: no (docs/rules/storefront.md:179 is a rule that asks for the current wording for content types; the fix keeps its reason)

findings.title: The store's slug is looked up by id again and again: the most-called statement in production
findings.evidence: select slug from commerce.stores where id = $1 ran 560,090 times, more than any other statement. It is written at 27 places (rg); 156 single-row reads of stores by id exist in 104 files. Page components know the store by id (GridPlace.owner, content-grid.ts:48-50), though the page was reached by slug. storeAndMarket() is not cached and not shared within a request, and has 11 callers: each grid, search, store part, recommendation and notice on a page asks again, and each cached grid function asks inside its own scope (content-grid.ts:166, 212, 310). A cached twin exists (storeSlugOf, menus.ts:283) and so does a per-request memo (perRequest, used in 4 files). The same habit for settings: aiFor() fetches the provider row on each of its 92 call sites' calls (237,563 calls in four shapes), and the one-row platform_settings is read by 43 statements in 29 files.
findings.cost: 7,180 round trips a day for a value that never changes; about 8 per page render (estimate: 560,090 calls against about 900 cold renders a day).
findings.who_pays: The server and the database on every render of a store page; each a round trip the page waits for.
findings.fix: Carry the slug in the place the page hands its components (GridPlace gets storeSlug), so nothing is looked up. Until then make storeAndMarket() call storeSlugOf() and wrap it in perRequest(). Give jobs the store they already loaded instead of its id. Keep an aiFor() answer per request with perRequest().
findings.saving: Estimate: nearly all 560,090 calls, and most of the 237,563 provider reads inside one request or job run.
findings.risk: Low. The slug of a store does not change (menus.ts:282 says so).

findings.title: Whole JSON documents are fetched where a field or a count is needed (61 page reads, 14 theme reads)
findings.evidence: The ten worst after DQ-2, DQ-6 and DQ-7. (1) theme-store.ts:137 reads every published theme with its whole snapshot to draw cards: 10,851 calls, 107,917 rows. (2) theme-store.ts:176 reads every version's whole snapshot of a theme to write a changelog. (3) theme-shots.ts:59, the same snapshots each minute: 35,101 calls. (4) pages.ts:136, the admin's Pages list, reads draft and published of every page to show a title, a state and a thumbnail. (5) accessibility.ts:120 reads every published page to count pages with issues. (6) green-claims.ts:54 reads every published page. (7) store-translate.ts:125 reads every page's draft. (8) stores.ts:232, the Store everyone reads (95 getStore calls in 68 files), carries seo, navigation, tracking, custom code, custom CSS, the theme and every menu with its items, for callers that need a slug or the languages. (9) fonts.ts:180 reads a family's whole stylesheet to pick one file name (42,211 calls for the two font reads). (10) analytics-speed.ts:116 loads every speed sample of 28 days, up to 10,000 a store day, to work out a 75th percentile in code. select * is the same habit in small: 138 in 80 files; the ones that run most are ai.ts:208 (237,563 calls), chat-agent.ts:93 (48,492), orders.ts:381 (orders has about 91 columns), cart.ts:251, media-library.ts:635 and 651, custom-fields.ts:96, owner-assistant.ts:234, cookie-scans.ts:178.
findings.cost: 128 s for the two theme reads; the rest is bytes and parse time on each call, not yet large. The speed report can load up to 280,000 rows for one screen.
findings.who_pays: The server (memory and parse) and the database; an owner on the Pages list, the theme store's visitors on a cold render.
findings.fix: Keep what cards and lists need beside the document, written when it is saved: for themes the looks, swatch and section style names at publish; for pages title, thumbnail and state as columns (or generated columns). Write the changelog from notes kept per version, not from snapshots. Compute the percentile in SQL (percentile_cont). Store the preload file name when a font is installed. Name the columns in the hot select * reads.
findings.saving: Estimate: the theme reads shrink from whole themes to card facts (most of 128 s); the admin Pages list and the speed report stop growing with document size and sample count.
findings.risk: Derived columns can drift from the document. Generated columns cannot; for the others a scan test over the writers, as store-writers.scan.test.ts does for stores.
findings.already_tracked: no (code review FD7, Open in step 3.15, names the width of orders but not these reads)

findings.title: Nothing counts queries: no budget per page or per tick, and production's statement statistics are not part of any routine
findings.evidence: rg finds no query budget, statement counter or mention of pg_stat_statements in src, e2e, scripts or docs. The ratchet (ratchet.baseline.json) holds four counts: casts, suppressions, unchecked reads and writes by id alone; none is about how many statements run or how much they return. The deploy routine in CLAUDE.md asks for the security and performance advisors after a migration, not for the statement statistics. Every finding above was visible in pg_stat_statements for weeks: a statement on an empty table called 278,393 times, 91,200 deletes that removed 782 rows, a slug lookup called 560,090 times.
findings.cost: No running cost of its own. It is why the others grew unseen: 22 scan tests guard other rules, none guards this.
findings.who_pays: Everyone later: each new section, job and cached read adds statements with no number to hold against.
findings.fix: (1) An integration test that counts statements (wrap the pool's query in the test) for one idle dispatcher tick, one idle run of each minute route, and one cold render of the demo store's front page and of the platform's home; keep the counts in the ratchet file so they may only fall. (2) Add to the after-deploy routine: read the 25 most-called and 25 costliest statements and explain any newcomer; the dispatcher can store that list weekly so the platform's Usage and limits page shows it. (3) Extend the scan tests: no new is not distinct from on store_id (DQ-8), no new minute schedule without a due test (DQ-1).
findings.saving: Not a direct saving. It keeps DQ-1 to DQ-10 from coming back and gives each a number to check the fix against.
findings.risk: A count that wobbles makes a flaky test. Count on a seeded database with caches cold, as the existing integration tests run.
findings.already_tracked: no (code review step 4.6 "Measure, then tune", Open, is the admin audit's and names no query count)

findings.title: Every server instance polls an empty translations table at start and each minute
findings.evidence: register() awaits startUi() before an instance takes requests; that runs select lang, count(*), max(updated_at) from commerce.ui_translations group by lang, then a timer repeats it every 60 s. Production: 278,393 calls, the second most-called statement, on a table that has never held a row (it is in the list of 255). ensureUi() already re-checks lazily when the answer is older than a minute, so the timer adds nothing on serverless.
findings.cost: 3,569 round trips a day, each tiny in database time. The first one sits in every cold start: an instance opens a connection and waits for the answer before serving (estimate: tens of milliseconds; not measured).
findings.who_pays: The first visitor served by a new instance; the database.
findings.fix: Drop the interval timer and rely on ensureUi(). When the last answer was "no languages", check again after 10 minutes, not 1. Do not block start-up on it once the first read has shown the table empty for this deployment: read it in the background and let t() fall back to English, which is what an empty table means anyway.
findings.saving: Estimate: from 3,569 calls a day to about one per instance start; one round trip less before a cold instance serves.
findings.risk: A language translated by AI would show up to 10 minutes late on other instances. reloadUi() already refreshes the instance that made the change.

findings.title: 341 loops hold a database call in their body; the costly ones are jobs that loop over sites
findings.evidence: A lexical scan finds 341 loops in 183 files with an awaited database call in the loop's own body (and 5 async map callbacks). Most run over a handful of rows by design (savepoints, per-language rows). The ten that matter: knowledge.ts:301 (per site: a full sync, an AI connection read, an embedding pass, every 5 minutes); media-library.ts:866 (per site: aiFor plus 2 to 4 statements, every 5 minutes; 49,842 stale checks); invoice-issue.ts:123 (two function calls per store, 9,909 each); embeddings.ts:120 (per store with its own AI); cart-reminders.ts:353 (one "bought since" lookup per due cart); theme-shots.ts:118 (one insert per missing shot); checkout.ts:1081, 1119 and 1150 and order-insert.ts:363 and 413 (one insert per fee, renewing line, gift card part, stock hold and variant, inside the order's transaction while it holds locks); products.ts:1207, 1241, 1632 and 1684 (per language or variant in a product save); house-customers.ts:387 and 481; standing-orders.ts:730 (7 calls in the body).
findings.cost: Per-site loops cost one or more round trips per site per tick: 60 sites today. The order's per-line inserts lengthen the time its locks are held by one round trip per line.
findings.who_pays: The database and the dispatcher every five minutes; a shopper at the moment of placing an order.
findings.fix: Per-site jobs: one set-based statement that returns only sites with work (as storesWithDocumentWork does at invoice-issue.ts:70) and a batch for the per-site reads (one aiFor read for all sites). Inserts of several rows: one insert with many value rows, as embeddings.ts:59-70 already does. The cart reminder's lookup: a left join in the query that finds the due carts.
findings.saving: Estimate: per-tick round trips of these jobs stop growing with the number of sites; an order with n lines saves about 2n round trips inside its transaction.
findings.risk: placeOrder is the money path: change it only with its tests, and with code review step 3.7.
findings.already_tracked: partly: code review step 3.7 "Stage placeOrder" (Open) restructures the order's writes; D320 already made a variant save "a few statements"

findings.title: 387 list reads have no limit by a heuristic count; a handful read a whole store's documents or samples
findings.evidence: Of 1,648 selects assigned to a const, 442 carry a limit and 387 return a list with no limit, no id or any() filter and no aggregate (heuristic). Most are bounded by their parent (an order's lines, a store's locations). The ten that are bounded only by how much a store has: pages.ts:136 (every page with both documents, for the admin list); pages.ts:668 (DQ-2); knowledge.ts:170 (DQ-6); accessibility.ts:120; green-claims.ts:46-55 (every active product's texts and every published page); store-translate.ts:125; analytics-speed.ts:116 (up to 28 days times 10,000 samples); activity.ts:155 (select distinct action over the audit log, to fill a filter); theme-store.ts:176 (every version's snapshot); owner-assistant.ts:234-235 (select * of every message and approval of a conversation). Rows loaded only to be counted are rare: 6 hits, see clean.
findings.cost: Small today (1,389 pages, 19,104 AI usage rows). Each of the ten returns rows in proportion to a store's whole content, so one large store makes its own screens slow.
findings.who_pays: An owner on the Pages list, the accessibility and claims screens and the activity filter; the server's memory.
findings.fix: Page the admin lists (the Pages list with the columns of DQ-10 and a limit, as step 1.13 will give every list). Compute in SQL what is computed from all rows (the speed percentile, the count of pages with issues kept at publish). Keep the audit log's distinct actions as a fixed list in code, which is where they are written. Load a conversation's newest messages first.
findings.saving: Estimate: these ten stop growing with a store's content; nothing measurable at today's sizes.
findings.risk: Paging changes what a list shows at once; it follows the shared list pattern of step 1.13.
findings.already_tracked: partly: code review step 1.13 "One way to search and page a list" (Open) covers paging admin lists; step 0.9 (Done) paged the storefront's listings
